title: Measurement Back-Action and Shot Noise
intro: Reading a quantum reservoir disturbs it, and each reading gives only a $\pm 1$ outcome, so a hardware QRC must both protect the memory carried by the state and pay in repetitions for every feature value. This page works through both costs quantitatively: what projective measurement does to the recurrence, the restart protocol, and how finite shots shrink memory capacity.

blocks.text: What a projective measurement does to the recurrence

The ideal reservoir update is $\rho_k = \mathcal{T}_{s_k}(\rho_{k-1})$, with features $x_{k,i}=\operatorname{Tr}(Z_i\rho_k)$. If after step $k$ we measure every qubit in the computational basis and obtain the bitstring $b$, the state becomes $|b\rangle\langle b|$. Averaged over outcomes, the state passed on is the dephased state

blocks.caption: Non-selective computational-basis measurement: all off-diagonal elements are erased.

blocks.text: So measuring everything every step replaces the map $\mathcal{T}_s$ by $\Delta\circ\mathcal{T}_s$. The reservoir now only carries a classical probability distribution over $2^n$ bitstrings from step to step, which is a Markov chain driven by the input. Worse, in a single run it does not even carry the distribution, it carries one sampled bitstring, so the next step's dynamics starts from a random basis state. Memory that lived in the coherences of $\rho$ is gone, and the information that survives has to pass through one sample per step.

This is why the textbook models of QRC (the Fujii–Nakajima spin reservoir among them, see Spin-Network Reservoirs (#/qrc/models/spin-network-reservoir)) assume the features are ensemble averages taken without disturbing the evolution. In NMR that is literally true (a macroscopic ensemble of identical molecules gives the average in one run); on a single-copy device it has to be emulated.
The restart protocol

The faithful emulation: for each output time $k$, prepare the initial state, feed inputs $s_1,\dots,s_k$, measure, and repeat $S$ times. Every run is a fresh, undisturbed copy of the trajectory up to $k$, so the estimate $\hat{x}_k$ is unbiased. The cost in evolution steps for a series of length $T$ is

With fading memory (the echo state property, see The Echo State Property (#/qrc/foundations/echo-state-property)) the state at time $k$ depends on inputs older than some window $w$ only negligibly. The run can then start at $k-w$ from any fixed state, and

The window $w$ should be a few times the decay time of the reservoir's state distance (the slope you see in the esp-contraction plot on the echo state property page): if the distance between two copies shrinks by a factor $e^{-1/\tau}$ per step, then $w \approx \tau \ln(1/\epsilon)$ makes the truncation error $\epsilon$. Mujal and coauthors (2023) analysed this rewinding protocol (replaying only the fading-memory window) and found it reaches ideal performance on memory and forecasting tasks. Both versions still need $S\,T$ separate runs, each ending in a measurement, and on most hardware the per-run overhead (reset, repetition delay, classical control) dominates the time per evolution step.
Shot noise on the features
Measuring $Z_i$ on a state with $\langle Z_i\rangle = x$ gives $+1$ with probability $(1+x)/2$. The sample mean of $S$ shots is unbiased with

Two facts make this cheaper than it looks. First, one computational-basis shot returns all $n$ bits at once, so all $\langle Z_i\rangle$ and all correlators $\langle Z_iZ_j\rangle$, $\langle Z_iZ_jZ_k\rangle,\dots$ come from the same $S$ shots: a feature vector of size $2^n-1$ (every diagonal Pauli) costs the same shots as one feature, although the higher-order correlators of a reservoir near the maximally mixed state are small and so have poor signal to noise. Second, $1-x^2$ is below 1 for any non-zero signal. Observables outside the $Z$ basis (say $\langle X_i\rangle$) need a basis rotation before measuring and therefore separate batches of shots.

What matters for learning is not $\sigma$ itself but its ratio to how much a feature moves as the input changes. In the 4-qubit reservoir of the numpy sample below, with $V=5$ virtual nodes, the $\langle Z_i\rangle$ traces vary over time with a standard deviation of only about 0.23. At $S=1000$ the shot noise is about 0.03, a signal-to-noise ratio near 8 per feature, and the memory capacity (delays 1 to 12) drops from 3.8 to 2.9. The plot runs the same model with a different random draw of couplings and inputs: it gives MC 5.1 with exact features and 3.3 at 1000 shots.

Try: set shots to 0 (exact) and note MC; then 100000, 10000, 1000, 100, 10. Capacity falls steadily as the shot budget shrinks, and faster the fewer shots you have: each tenfold cut removes about 0.2 of capacity near $10^5$ shots but about 1 near 100, and the long delays (whose signal is weakest in the features) go first. Then raise V with shots fixed at 1000: more virtual nodes still help, because the readout averages noise across more features, but less than in the exact case.

blocks.text: Shot noise as an implicit regulariser

Independent zero-mean noise $\eta$ of variance $\sigma^2$ added to the training features turns the least-squares objective, in expectation, into ridge regression: for $T$ training rows, $\mathbb{E}\Vert y - (X+\eta)w\Vert^2 = \Vert y - Xw\Vert^2 + T\sigma^2\Vert w\Vert^2$. So training on noisy features automatically shrinks the weights, which is why a QRC readout fitted on hardware data is often less over-fitted than one fitted on exact simulated features. But the test features are noisy too, and that noise passes straight through the weights to the output, with variance $\sigma^2\Vert w\Vert^2$. The two effects together are why the memory function decays faster with fewer shots: recalling an old input needs large, finely balanced weights on small feature differences, exactly what noise forbids.
Practical consequence: tune the ridge parameter on noisy features, never on exact ones. A readout regularised for exact simulation will have weights that amplify shot noise on the device.
Worked problems

blocks.title: Shot noise on one feature
blocks.text: A feature has true value $\langle Z_1\rangle = 0.6$. What is the standard deviation of its estimate from $S=1000$ shots, and how many shots bring it below 0.01?

blocks.title: Full versus windowed restart
blocks.text: A series has $T=500$ inputs, you take $S=2000$ shots per output time, and the reservoir forgets inputs older than $w=15$ steps. Count the evolution steps for the full and the windowed restart protocols and their ratio.
blocks.hint: Sum $k$ from 1 to $T$ for the full protocol.

blocks.title: Choosing the window
blocks.text: Two copies of a reservoir fed the same inputs approach each other in trace distance by a factor 0.7 per step. How long a window $w$ keeps the truncation error below $10^{-3}$ of the initial distance?
solution: After $w$ steps the distance is $0.7^w$ of its start.
